title: Alexa, Meet Humanitarian Data
html:
Over the past couple years, OCHA has been moving to a micro-services architecture for its systems. Essentially, we are separating the front-end and back-end of tools and websites using APIs. One of the benefits becomes that tools are able to call on the back-ends of other systems. Perhaps our most obvious example is the ReliefWeb Crises app which calls upon many of the OCHA micro-services along with several external APIs to compile itself.

The benefit of separating front-end from back-end has been quite obvious from an application stand-point. But, more recently, I have realized that micro-services maybe provide another benefit – improved accessibility to humanitarian data.

A couple months ago, Jeremy Andrews joined me in the OCHA Digital Services team. I asked him to see if he could surface the ReliefWeb Crises numbers through Amazon’s Alexa. Yes, I mean accessing information about crisis affected countries exclusively with voice commands.  No mobile phone, no tablet and no computer. The video below shows the result after about 10-15 hours of development work by Jeremy.

Embedded video: watch on YouTube

[Video link: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Tz4MIhpfMnA]

Although accessibility will remain an extremely important factor for websites and tools, making use of micro-services (APIs) and artificial intelligence (e.g. Alexa) may not only provide a new frontier to explore humanitarian information for everyone, but may even help make such data become ubiquitous for all decision makers.

Andrej
teaser: What happens when humanitarian data meets Alexa? An experiment surfacing ReliefWeb Crises numbers through OCHA's micro-services.
seo_description: How OCHA's move to micro-services made it possible to surface ReliefWeb Crises figures on Amazon Alexa and improve access to humanitarian data.
